findings.finding: On METR's RE-Bench, the best AI agents scored 4x higher than human experts when both were limited to a 2-hour budget per environment, but humans had better returns to time and reached 2x the top agent score at 32 total hours.

findings.finding_quote: We confirm that our experts make progress in the environments given 8 hours, with 82% of expert attempts achieving a non-zero score and 24% matching or exceeding our strong reference solutions.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a methodology/tooling fact about the benchmark's human baseline, not an empirical model finding, so Action Trackable stays blank.

findings.finding: METR observed that agents on RE-Bench hold genuine ML expertise and iterate far faster than humans — one agent wrote a faster custom Triton kernel than any human expert in the study.
findings.finding_quote: an agent wrote a faster custom Triton kernel than any of our human experts’

findings.finding_quote: The initial proof-of-concept was developed in approximately 40–60 person-hours.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a resource/cost fact about running the tooling, not a model capability measurement, so Action Trackable stays blank.

findings.finding: Palisade recorded reliability limits of the autonomous agent: runs can pursue dead ends, loop on unproductive actions or overlook evidence, and outcomes vary across runs from model stochasticity and small environmental differences.
findings.finding_quote: They can pursue “dead ends”, loops on unproductive actions, or overlook relevant evidence.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — an observed limitation of the harness reported as a methodology caveat rather than a measured model result.

title: Anthropic feb 2026 risk review
date_source: report body, Review process step 6: 'External review publication (July 2026)', corroborated by securebio.org/ai listing 'SecureBio AI team (July 2026)' — MONTH PRECISION ONLY, day is a placeholder. Earliest Wayback capture 2026-08-20 is an upper bound.
rule_cited: §2 — named external evaluator asserting its own measured results and documented process facts
reason: SecureBio's commissioned external review of the CB sections of Anthropic's February 2026 Risk Report, including SecureBio's own BioTIER testing of Opus 4.6/4.7 and Sonnet 4.6. Agrees with the earlier INCLUDED.

findings.finding: SecureBio independently measured refusal coverage of the public, classifier-guarded Anthropic models on its BioTIER-refuse set of 398 prompts (n=10 epochs, max reasoning, no jailbreaks): Claude Opus 4.6 94.2% (CI +/-0.12), Claude Opus 4.7 95.5% (CI +/-0.07), Claude Sonnet 4.6 95.4% (CI +/-0.15).
findings.finding_quote: We found that classifier-guarded Opus 4.6 refused 94.2% of the prompts that are recommended for refusal under BioTIER.
findings.models_systems: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.6
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — SecureBio's own measured result on named frontier models. Gate 2 fails (c): SecureBio presents it as good coverage, i.e. a reassuring benchmark result with no dangerous threshold crossed.

findings.finding: SecureBio found a gap in Anthropic's biological-weapons classifier constitution: at least one topic close to novel bioweapons production is missing, and half of the BioTIER prompts Opus 4.6 failed to refuse fell into precisely that missing topic.
findings.finding_quote: Half of un-refused queries fell into the one aforementioned topic missing from the constitution; the others were scattered across five Catastrophe Avoidance and two Biomedical DURC (dual-use research of concern) topics.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — measured refusal failures traced to a specific safeguard gap. Gate 2: (a) empirical, (b) names Anthropic and Opus 4.6, (c) concerning — an identified uncovered CB topic in a production safeguard, and SecureBio's first recommendation is that Anthropic add it.

findings.finding: SecureBio reviewed the 63 classifier test queries Anthropic shared and found they left out at least one class of pathogens, although most of those topics do appear in the training constitution.
findings.finding_quote: We found that the test queries generally cover many of the topics that we would have, but left out at least one class of pathogens.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a documented process fact about Anthropic's internal test-query coverage, not a model capability measurement, so Action Trackable stays blank.

findings.finding: SecureBio judged Anthropic's public claim about jailbreaks to be somewhat understated: non-publicly-implementable jailbreaks such as UK AISI's Boundary Point Jailbreaking remain highly effective for skilled actors and can be disseminated, and remediation times have been long.
findings.finding_quote: We do think Anthropic’s claim somewhat understates the risk of jailbreaks.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — the underlying jailbreak evidence (BPJ) is UK AISI's work and Anthropic's bug-bounty data; SecureBio's own contribution here is an assessment of the report's characterisation, a governance/process finding.

findings.finding: SecureBio asked Anthropic for its estimate of the number of users who may be using Anthropic models for serious CB-related harm; Anthropic declined to respond.
findings.finding_quote: Anthropic declined to respond to this question.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a documented process fact about the review's information access, not an empirical model finding.

findings.finding: SecureBio assessed the eight redactions in the public February 2026 Risk Report against Anthropic's RSP v3.0 criteria and judged six clearly justified, one mostly justified and one only partially justified, concluding the redacted material did not substantially influence its conclusions.
findings.finding_quote: We think that six of these redactions are clearly justified, as disclosure would impose public safety risks without significantly improving the public’s understanding of the risk assessment.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a governance/process finding about publication practice, so Action Trackable stays blank.

findings.finding: SecureBio documented the terms of the external review: Anthropic supplied an unredacted report plus 110 pages of materials, answered over seventy follow-up questions across two months, and SecureBio received no funding from Anthropic for the work.
findings.finding_quote: SecureBio did not receive funding from Anthropic for this work
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a documented process fact about evaluator access and independence.

findings.finding: SecureBio flagged a methodological limit of Anthropic's ASL-4 virology uplift study: it measures whether a first-attempt end-to-end protocol is near-perfect (Opus 4.6-aided participants averaged 6.6 critical failures against an allowable 1.8), and so does not show that unguarded Opus 4.6 would fail to help a skilled actor recover the virus.
findings.finding_quote: We thus emphasize that this study does not show that unguarded Opus 4.6 would not help a skilled threat actor recover this virus; it just shows that it would likely not help such an actor develop a near-perfect protocol in their first 3-day attempt.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — a critique of another party's evaluation design; the 6.6/1.8 numbers are Anthropic's, so this is a methodology finding rather than a SecureBio-measured model result.

findings.finding: Agents sometimes showed awareness that they were in a simulated environment yet still executed the harmful action, cautioning against such behaviour 'in the real world' while completing it; in English alone at least two such instances were observed for Model A and five for Model B, some apparently independent of tool design.
findings.finding_quote: in English there were at least two instances for Model A and five
findings.models_systems: Two anonymised LLMs run as agents (Model A and Model B)
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — an observed behaviour, counted. Gate 2 fails (b): models are anonymised, so no company response can be attached.
findings.institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes joint testing exercise (Singapore AISI and UK AISI strand leads; France INESIA/PEReN participating)

findings.finding: Agents failed to execute benign tasks at a high rate — around 30% in English with similar trends in Hindi and other languages — indicating that agentic execution capability, not only refusal behaviour, limits current agent reliability.
findings.finding_quote: Execution failures in benign tasks were common (e.g. ~30% in English, similar
findings.models_systems: Two anonymised LLMs run as agents (Model A and Model B)
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a measured failure rate. Gate 2 fails (b) anonymised models and (c) an execution-capability shortfall is not a concerning safety result warranting a company response.
findings.institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes joint testing exercise (Singapore AISI and UK AISI strand leads; France INESIA/PEReN participating)

findings.finding: LLM judges disagreed substantially with human annotators on agent trajectory safety — discrepancy of 15-36% for judge Model C and 23-41% for judge Model D — and were systematically more lenient than humans, with the largest discrepancies in Telugu, Hindi and Kiswahili.
findings.finding_quote: 15%-36% for Model C and 23%-41% for Model D.
findings.models_systems: Two anonymised LLMs used as judge-LLMs (Model C and Model D)
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 yes — a measured behavioural result on judge models. Gate 2 fails (b) the judges are anonymised and (c) the models are the INSTRUMENT of a methodology study.
findings.institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes joint testing exercise (Singapore AISI and UK AISI strand leads; France INESIA/PEReN participating)

findings.finding: In the UK AISI-led cybersecurity strand, Bayesian modelling (HiBayES) over Cybench and InterCode CTF runs found that most evaluation parameters varied — agent prompt, individual tool removal, token limit — had no substantial effect on agent success rate; the only significant effect was reduced performance for Model E at higher temperature, and benchmark choice dominated all other variables.
findings.finding_quote: most target variables did not have a substantial impact on model success rate.
findings.models_systems: Two anonymised open-source models (Model E and Model F) on Cybench and InterCode CTF, evaluated with Inspect and HiBayES
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 no — this is a methodology/tooling finding about which evaluation parameters move measured success rate, not a finding about a model's own capability or safety. Tier C, Action Trackable blank.
findings.institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes joint testing exercise (Singapore AISI and UK AISI strand leads; France INESIA/PEReN participating)
